lesson.title: More Than a Growling Stomach: The Biology and Psychology of Hunger
lesson.summary: Eating behavior is regulated by an interacting system of hormonal signals like ghrelin and leptin, brain structures including the hypothalamus, and psychological and environmental cues, making hunger both a textbook example of drive-reduction theory and a clear illustration of that theory's limits.
lesson.body:
Hunger is one of the clearest real world examples of drive-reduction theory in action. A physiological deficit, the body's need for calories and nutrients, creates an uncomfortable internal state, and that state pushes the organism to act, to seek out and consume food, in order to restore a stable internal balance, or homeostasis. Few everyday experiences map onto the language of drive-reduction theory as directly as the felt urgency of being genuinely hungry.

That drive is coordinated in large part through hormonal signals, most notably ghrelin and leptin, working in something like a feedback loop. Ghrelin is released mainly by the stomach when it is empty, it rises before meals and signals the brain to initiate hunger and food seeking behavior. Leptin is released by fat tissue in proportion to how much fat is stored in the body, it signals satiety and helps suppress appetite as fat stores are adequately replenished. Together, rising ghrelin and rising leptin act as opposing signals that help keep the body's energy supply within a roughly stable range over time.

The hypothalamus is where much of this signaling gets translated into felt hunger or satiety and into eating behavior itself. Classic research pointed to two hypothalamic regions playing something like opposite roles, the lateral hypothalamus contributing to the onset of hunger, and the ventromedial hypothalamus contributing to the sense of fullness that ends a meal. It is worth being explicit that this simple dual center picture, while a genuinely useful starting point and still commonly taught, is a simplification. Later research has shown that feeding regulation actually involves a more distributed network of hypothalamic nuclei and neural circuits working together with hormonal signals like ghrelin and leptin, rather than two isolated on and off switches.

Eating behavior is also shaped by far more than internal physiology. The sight or smell of appealing food, social eating occasions, learned habits and routines, stress, and simple availability can all drive eating even in the absence of a strong physiological deficit, and can just as easily suppress eating despite one. This is part of why hunger, while a strong example of drive-reduction theory, also reveals its limits, external, learned pulls toward food, the same kind of incentive driven pull described in incentive theory, matter alongside the internal push of physiological need.

Finally, many researchers describe the body as defending something like a set point, a fairly stable weight range that it works to maintain over time through compensatory adjustments in hunger, satiety, and metabolism when intake changes. The precise mechanisms behind this tendency, and how flexible or fixed any individual's set point actually is, remain areas of ongoing research rather than fully settled science.
